Authors: Henri Vermeersch, Xander Pottier, Quinten Norga, Thomas de Ruijter, Ingrid Verbauwhede
Summary: Lattice-based post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) rely heavily on the number theoretic transform (NTT) for efficient polynomial multiplication. While GPUs and FPGAs have been widely explored for NTT acceleration, neural processing units (NPUs), a rapidly growing class of AI accelerators, remain largely unexplored for cryptographic workloads. In this work, we develop a methodology for accelerating the NTT on NPUs, using AMD’s AI Engine (AIE) architecture as a representative NPU to develop and benchmark it. At its core is manual loop fission, in which large and complex loops are split into smaller primitives, enabling highly efficient software pipelining and avoiding memory stalls or register spilling. Applying it, we develop efficient Barrett reduction primitives and use these to construct three high-throughput, low-latency NTT implementations (radix-2, radix-4, and radix-8), achieving significant performance gains over the AIE compiler and prior literature. On AMD’s first-generation AIE specifically, we achieve speedups of $8.27\times$ to $13.2\times$ in throughput and $2.44\times$ to $10.3\times$ in latency per AIE tile in comparison with prior work. Our implementations support arbitrary NTT-friendly moduli and polynomial sizes up to degree 4096 for 14-bit moduli and 2048 for 30-bit moduli. Finally, we discuss the portability of our techniques to other NPU architectures, and identify which architectural features are most beneficial for NTT acceleration.

item.title: edaBits in the Exponent (edaBitE) and Issuer-Hiding Blind Signatures from ML-DSA and VOLE-in-the-Head
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2473
Authors: Carsten Baum, Marvin Beckmann
Summary: Blind signatures let a user obtain a signature by interacting with an issuer that controls the signing key, while the issuer never sees the message. They form the basis of anonymous credentials, which are the centerpiece of privacy-preserving digital identification to be deployed widely in the coming years. Existing plausibly quantum-secure blind signatures rely on bespoke cryptographic constructions, instead of standardized ones. This is dissatisfying from a cryptographic perspective, and also leads to practical issues: secret signing keys are often stored in secure elements, in which case only signature algorithms supported by certified secure elements can be the basis for deployed protocols.
We give the first blind signature whose issuer runs a NIST-standardized post-quantum signature scheme unmodified. Issuance is just an ML-DSA signature on a commitment, and the blind signature is a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge, using the VOLE-in-the-head zero-knowledge proof system, of the ML-DSA signature. Security reduces to the EUF-CMA security of ML-DSA and to the proof system, with no new assumptions. A blind signature is about $1$ MB and takes under a second to produce and half a second to verify. Issuer-hiding and selective disclosure of signed attributes can easily be added on top for a few tens of kilobytes, at a proof size essentially independent of how many issuers the list names.
Underlying the construction is edaBitE, a novel batch consistency check between binary and prime-field commitments. In a non-interactive proof, the existing edaBits checks it replaces would be the single largest item in the blind signature. We believe that edaBitE is of independent interest.

item.title: Nowhere Man: Device Binding for Post-Quantum Anonymous Credentials
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2472
Authors: Calvin Abou Haidar, Ryo Kikuchi, Octavio Perez-Kempner, Marcel Tiepelt
Summary: Anonymous credentials are seeing widespread deployment. Notably, the European Commission plans to roll out age-verification solutions based on anonymous credentials by the end of 2026. Similarly, Google open-sourced Longfellow, a zero-knowledge proof system that lifts the standardized mobile Driver License framework into a full-fledged anonymous credentials, and is currently being integrated with Google Wallet.
Any secure deployment of anonymous credentials must address two major challenges: 1) provide guarantees against credential sharing, and 2) support proof-of-personhood. The standard approach adopted by the industry to address both is device binding, which is mandatory for mDL and was only recently formalized for anonymous credentials by Friedrichs et al. (Eurocrypt '26). Simply put, the idea is to have the user's phone Secure Element sign a fresh challenge from the verifier, and to prove knowledge of this signature in zero-knowledge at each credential presentation.
To date, all existing approaches, including Vega (S&P '26), have only considered non-post-quantum solutions based on legacy signature schemes. Crucial for near-term deployments and adoption is to work with standardized post-quantum signature schemes, such as ML-DSA, which were not designed for privacy. Because of this, solutions based on general non-interactive zero-knowledge proof systems (e.g., Longfellow) appear to be needed. This genericity, however, requires proving complex statements, significantly impacting proving time.
In this work, we present a modular device binding protocol tailored to work with ML-DSA. We avoid the pitfalls of the generic approach by leveraging the structure of ML-DSA resulting in an efficient solution, but retaining the security underlying the post-quantum standard. Our most efficient variants additionally rely on a weak-MLWR assumption for unlinkability, which can be removed at the cost of lower efficiency. While tailored for ML-DSA and requiring no modification to the FIPS~204 signing interface, our solution is modular enough to be integrated with different anonymous credential schemes, allowing real-world solutions to pick the most efficient building blocks. To demonstrate the feasibility of our solution, we provide a proof-of-concept implementation.

item.title: Connecting Cryptanalytic Distinguishers through Divisibility
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2471
Authors: Hosein Hadipour
Summary: Integral distinguishers can reveal more than a zero-sum property: the number of ones in an output component may be divisible by a high power of $2$, rather than merely being even. To exploit this divisibility, we relate linear, integral, differential-linear, and restricted differential sums through two-way conversions with explicit divisibility guarantees and data complexity, recovering established links as special cases. We derive exact random-permutation probabilities and rigorous bounds to quantify the distinguishing strength while accounting for dependencies between output conditions. To discover these properties, we develop automated MILP/SAT models that use complete-round Walsh coefficients or combine Walsh and ultrametric representations to obtain stronger bounds. These weighted models prove finite divisibility even when compatible trails exist, beyond what trail-existence tests alone can establish. For differential-linear sums, we show that combining differential and linear propagation with local DLCT zeros can give false zero-correlation claims. We address this limitation with exact mix-basis models that establish zero correlation and finite divisibility. To complement these symbolic methods, we provide a black-box algorithm using exact histograms and the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform to search all output masks for selected input conditions and identify zeros and finite divisibility properties. Our MILP/SAT models significantly improve the divisibility bounds reported by Beyne and Verbauwhede in 674 cases across the SIMON family, as well as for PRESENT, without trail enumeration and at unchanged data complexity, e.g., from $2^5$ to $2^{11}$ on 9-round SIMON32 and from $2^6$ to $2^{22}$ on 10-round SIMON48. To our knowledge, we are the first to prove higher divisibility for 8-round SPECK and for BEANIE, with new bounds for GIFT-64 and Ascon and exact counts for SKINNY-64. Our black-box searches reveal new properties on RC5, ChiLow-32, KeeLoq, and KATAN32, including output-bit combinations missed by single-bit searches, and lead us to introduce probabilistic divisibility.

item.title: Refined Application of the XL Algorithm within the Algebraic Approach to the Regular Syndrome Decoding Problem
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2470
Authors: Hiroki Furue, Yusuke Aikawa
Summary: The Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP) is a fundamental mathematical problem underlying code-based cryptography, which is considered a promising candidate for post-quantum cryptography. The Regular Syndrome Decoding Problem (RSDP) is a variant of the SDP in which the error vector follows a specific block-wise structure. Recent developments in RSDP-based cryptographic schemes have led to a wider variety of parameter settings, making it increasingly important to evaluate the complexity of solving the RSDP over a broad range of parameters. One of the main approaches to solving the RSDP is the algebraic approach, which transforms a given RSDP instance into a polynomial system and solves it using algebraic techniques such as the XL algorithm. In this work, we construct and analyze algebraic algorithms for the RSDP by combining and extending techniques used in existing algebraic approaches. Our algorithms mainly follow the framework of the hybrid algorithm proposed by Wang et al., while allowing an arbitrary solving degree $d$ in the application of the XL algorithm. We further consider two variants: an XFL-based method that combines partial Gaussian elimination with variable guessing, and a WXL-based method that exploits the sparsity of the Macaulay matrix. Our complexity analysis for various parameter settings shows that, for some fixed values of $n$ and $k$, the WXL-based variant using a larger solving degree $d>2$ is particularly efficient when the block size $\beta$ is sufficiently small, while the original hybrid algorithm becomes more efficient as $\beta$ increases.

item.title: Accelerating Pollard Rho with GPU Field Arithmetic on NVIDIA Blackwell
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2469
Authors: Adam Buran, Kevin Nguyen
Summary: We show how far Pollard rho can be accelerated on current NVIDIA GPUs by rebuilding its field arithmetic around the hardware, with the Certicom challenge ECC2K-130, the Koblitz curve $y^2+xy=x^3+1$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2^{131}}$ with an expected cost of $2^{60.9}$ iterations, as the benchmark. None of the speedup comes from changing the algorithm. It comes from a packed normal-basis representation in which every Frobenius power is a permutation network instead of a chain of squarings; from the carry-less multiply that CUDA 13.3 exposes in PTX (clmad), which forms a 131-bit product in six instructions; from three-input logic instructions for everything around it; and from a batch size, launch geometry and compact tiled state chosen by measurement against the pipes they load. Across sixteen paired steps, each held to a rule written down before it ran, these take one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell from a $0.85$ billion iterations per second bitsliced control to $14.64$ in the audited campaign build, a $17.2\times$ gain (representation and arithmetic $6.3\times$, geometry $1.5\times$, memory layout $1.3\times$, clmad $1.2\times$), and a later build reaches $15.88$. That is about $230$ times the best published 2010 GPU kernel per card and puts the whole challenge under five GPU-years: five cards expect a solution within a year, a thousand in about three days. The gains depend on the die. clmad issues ten to eighteen times faster per SM-clock on the data-centre parts than on the workstation part, so the same change can win on one Blackwell part and lose on another; we report twelve GPUs from Turing to Blackwell per card, per SM and per dollar, and the CPU instruction sets that play the same role. Upper bounds derived from measured pipe rates leave about $1.5\times$ of headroom on one RTX PRO 6000, at $24$–$26$ billion iterations per second for any walk with one addition per step. The same levers applied to Pollard rho on NIST P-256 and P-384 on the same card give $1.52\times$ and $2.61\times$, to $1.632$ and $0.548$ billion iterations per second, which still leaves P-256 about $6\cdot10^{21}$ card-years away. We also separate the $\sigma$-walk from a table walk whose $20.08$ was measured under a cycle rule later found unsound (the exact rule runs at $8.24$), measure the walk constant at $2^{60.91}$–$2^{60.92}$ iterations, and report an FPGA engine at $8.25$ billion iterations per second on one AWS F2 and a campaign that walked $2^{56.68}$ iterations, $5.4\%$ of the expected work. Every number cites an evidence record; the code, data, evidence and a Dockerfile whose image starts the ECC2K-130 walk are at https://github.com/aburan28/rho-blackwell. None of this improves on the generic-group bound, and we do not claim that it does.

item.title: FlatMerkle: Logarithmic-Space Inclusion Proofs over a Single Linear Hash Stream
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2468
Authors: Sergio Demian Lerner
Summary: Merkle trees are the standard way to obtain logarithmic-size, logarithmic-time inclusion proofs over a large dataset, but they require a tree-shaped hash structure distinct from the ordinary, linear (Merkle--Damg\aa rd) hashing that most deployed systems -- including Bitcoin's own transaction and witness hashing -- actually perform. We present FlatMerkle, a construction that achieves the same asymptotic guarantees, $O(\log N)$ proof size and $O(\log N)$ verification time, over a single ordinary linear hash stream, by periodically re-injecting the hash function's own past internal states (``checkpoints'') back into the stream as ordinary message content. The result is a flat byte sequence whose digest is a single, unmodified invocation of the underlying hash function -- syntactically an ordinary digest of an ordinary byte string, not a distinguishable commitment format -- while still supporting compact inclusion proofs for any element, and compact proofs that a published file is malformed, so that an honest party can always answer a malicious committer in logarithmic space. We give the recursive construction, a closed-form formula locating any element in the structured stream, worked examples with illustrations, a security reduction to free-start collision resistance of the hash function's compression step, an optimal element-size analysis for both a flexible toy primitive and real SHA-256, a batched multi-element proof construction, a measured construction-speed comparison against Merkle trees, a concrete application to committing data inside a Bitcoin transaction annex (BIP-341), a design sketch using that application as a data-availability layer for an optimistic Bitcoin rollup, a from-scratch gas-cost comparison, on Ethereum, Rootstock, and Arbitrum, of an in-contract FlatMerkle commitment against an in-contract Merkle tree, tracing the three chains' differing verdicts to specific protocol design choices rather than to anything intrinsic to either construction, and a comparison against the closest prior art we are aware of, authenticated append-only skip lists.

item.title: DPF-SGD: Byzantine-Robust Differentially Private Federated SGD with Exact Optimality Guarantees
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2467
Authors: Likang Lu, Jiaxin Wu
Summary: Federated optimization enables collaborative learning over decentralized data but is accompanied by significant privacy risks due to the exchange of model updates. While differential privacy (DP) provides formal protection, optimization accuracy is often degraded, and robustness becomes particularly limited in the presence of Byzantine agents. A Byzantine-robust, differentially private federated SGD algorithm, DPF-SGD, is proposed, in which private step sizes are integrated with a DP noise–decay schedule to regulate gradient updates. To further enhance robustness, a privacy-preserving comparative elimination (PPCE) filter is developed to suppress Byzantine contributions during aggregation while preserving privacy guarantees. Almost sure convergence to the global optimum under ϵ-differential privacy is established, despite persistent noise and adversarial behavior. Experiments on synthetic and MNIST datasets demonstrate oneto two-order-of-magnitude reductions in final optimization error relative to DP baselines.

item.title: Trustless Bitcoin Vaults
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2466
Authors: Lukas Aumayr, Xinshu Dong, Runchao Han, Srivatsan Sridhar, David Tse, Nikhil Vanjani
Summary: Bitcoin (BTC) is the largest crypto asset, yet the Bitcoin blockchain offers few applications in which BTC can be used. A standard approach to make BTC useful is bridging: BTC is deposited on the Bitcoin chain and a wrapped asset is minted on a chain such as Ethereum, where it can be used in smart contract applications. Unfortunately, all Bitcoin bridges to date require trust assumptions on a centralized party or a committee running the bridge to enable withdrawals of the deposited BTC, including state-of-the-art BitVM bridges.
In this paper, we observe that while bridges are application-agnostic, most BTC holders are interested in collateral-based applications, where BTC is deposited as collateral, and only the depositor or a set of known counterparties can withdraw the asset. For this class of applications, we propose a primitive, Trustless Bitcoin Vaults, that guarantees that the BTC depositor or the counterparties can withdraw the deposited BTC following only the logic of the application smart contract without trusting any third party. We present a protocol that achieves the security guarantees of this primitive and instantiate it for a lending application where the deposited BTC is used as collateral to borrow against a set of liquidators on the Aave v4 smart contracts on Ethereum. Our mainnet experiments show that at the current Bitcoin price and fee rate, a deposit costs about \$0.7 in fees while a withdrawal costs at most \$7.7. Our construction is built on recent advances in efficient proof verification for Bitcoin.
