item.title: A Graph-Based Analysis of Comparability, Scale, and Attribution in Private Transformer Inference
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2464
Authors: Souvik Das, Ariful Azad, Nitesh Saxena
Summary: Rising privacy concerns around large language models have accelerated research in private Transformer inference (PTI). Synthesizing the empirical claims in this line of research, however, is hindered by multi-dimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts. In this work, we systematize the field by constructing an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges. A three-tiered analysis of this graph illuminates the state of private inference. Node-level attribution shows that cryptographic progress drives performance gains across most systems, yet always co-occurs with other factors (model fidelity, hardware, cost accounting). Edge-level auditing shows that only 1 of 1891 candidate system pairs is directly comparable under shared assumptions. Finally, graph-level analysis shows that the scaling frontier of private inference has plateaued at 13B parameters and projects the cost of deploying current PTI techniques on production-scale Transformers. Overall, this graph-based framework equips the community to evaluate PTI claims transparently and channel technical speedups into deployment-scale private inference.

item.title: Tree-BTE: Batched Threshold Encryption using Additive Homomorphism
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2463
Authors: Amit Agarwal, Sourav Das, Babak Poorebrahim Gilkalaye, Benny Pinkas, Peter Rindal
Summary: Batched threshold encryption (BTE) enables a committee of servers to jointly decrypt any chosen subset of ciphertexts from a large pool, while all remaining ciphertexts stay private. BTE is a key building block for encrypted mempools, where transactions are encrypted until block inclusion to mitigate maximal extractable value (MEV). We give a new tree-based BTE construction from two simple building blocks which support additive homomorphism: a symmetric-key encryption scheme that is homomorphic over key and message space, and a thresholdizable public-key encryption scheme that is homomorphic over message space. These building blocks can be instantiated under a wide variety of assumptions including DDH, DCR, LWR and even LWE for post-quantum security.
In our scheme, each ciphertext is associated with an index from an appropriate index space. We implement the DDH-based instantiation. Given an aggregated batch of 1,000 messages over a small 1024 sized index space, each server performs about 41~ms of single-thread computation, including a 100-of-300 threshold decryption. We also partially implement an RLWE-based post-quantum instantiation over a \(2^{128}\) sized index space for negligible collision probability among indices. A batch of 1024 messages uses approximately 0.89 MB per ciphertext and 20 seconds of single-thread decryption per server.

item.title: Hybrid Quantum–Computational Key Distribution with Reduced Assumptions (Short Paper)
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2462
Authors: Jean Snyman, Ioana Boureanu, Daniel Gardham
Summary: The HM-QCT protocol, presented by Mazzoncini et al. in 2025, uses a unique feature of quantum information to achieve quantum key distribution (QKD) with secret-key rates beyond standard constructions. The protocol has been designed in the hybrid quantum–computational time-lock (QCT) security model which imposes two independent (but related) restrictions on the attacker: (1) a computationally secure encryption scheme which a successful attacker must break within a narrow timeframe and (2) an assumption that the attacker can only store quantum information with low fidelity.
We first review the protocol and its two-assumption model by presenting, in explicit form, the two natural “harvest now, decrypt later” strategies against it, one using quantum memory and one using classical memory. We show how each is excluded by exactly one of the two assumptions, so that harvesting resistance rests on their conjunction and on the presumed existence of a technological gap: the adversary's quantum memory must decohere much faster than the time it takes to break the short-term encryption.
Finally, we introduce HM-PRF, a variant that replaces the short-term encryption with a pseudorandom function (PRF), evaluated locally. By eliminating the transmission of enciphered classical information, the adversary does not need to race an impending expiry event. We compare the security of our construction against the original and argue that our PRF-based assumption yields a more realistic adversary. It simply requires the existence of one-way functions rather than a predicted lasting limitation of quantum computation and memory technology.

item.title: Leakage-Resilient Incompressible Cryptography: Constructions and Barriers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2461
Authors: KAARTIK BHUSHAN, Rishab Goyal, Venkata Koppula, Varun Narayanan, Manoj Prabhakaran, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree
Summary: We introduce Leakage-Resilient Incompressible cryptography, which simultaneously addresses two variants of side-channel attacks that have been tackled in theoretical cryptography. Leakage-resilience seeks to provide security against an adversary who learns a part of the secret-key and the entire ciphertext or signature; conversely, incompressible cryptography provides security against an adversary who learns the entire secret-key, but only a part of the ciphertext or signature. However, constructions in either of these security models can fail against an attack in the other model. In this work, we define a new model of security that subsumes both leakage-resilient cryptography and incompressible cryptography, and we present several non-trivial positive and negative results.
On the positive side, first we present a transformation from incompressible symmetric-key encryption (SKE) to leakage-resilient incompressible SKE in the information-theoretic setting. Next, as one of our main results, we construct a leakage-resilient incompressible public-key encryption (PKE), combining an incompressible SKE and a new primitive that we call leakage-resilient non-committing key encapsulation mechanism (LR-NC-KEM).
While an information-theoretic incompressible SKE suitable for use in both these constructions already exists in the literature (Dziembowski, CRYPTO 2006), we present a new construction achieving ciphertext-rate $\frac{1}{2}$ and compression-rate $\frac{1}{2}$, using an appropriate notion of invertible extractors; this leads to corresponding improvements in the final parameters we obtain in these constructions. We also construct a leakage-resilient incompressible signature scheme in the classical random oracle model, assuming $(\mathsf{DCR}\text{ or }\mathsf{LWE})$ and the Decisional Linear assumption, with signature-rate and compression-rate $1-o(1)$ and leakage-rate $1$.
On the negative side, we show barriers to significantly improving the parameters we obtain, by showing impossibility of basing the security of such improved schemes on blackbox reductions.
Apart from the general framework and the specific results we obtain, some of the intermediate tools that we define and instantiate, like LR-NC-KEM and invertible extractors, may be of independent interest.

item.title: Cube Attacks with Elimination Strategy: Key Recovery Attacks on Trivium
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2460
Authors: Haoran Li, Shichang Wang, Meicheng Liu, Willi Meier, Dongdai Lin
Summary: In this paper, we present a novel framework for cube attacks named cube attacks with elimination strategy. The core idea is to find specific key conditions and cubes such that their superpolies under these key conditions can be efficiently computed. By recovering these conditional superpolies, we can solve the corresponding equation system and thereby retrieve key information. If a sufficient number of such key conditions can be found, the attack can be extended to a larger key space. To apply this framework in practical attacks, we propose the following techniques.
First, we propose a nested coefficient solver that combines variable substitution and symbolic computation to efficiently recover superpolies, and present the conditional monomial prediction technique to rapidly recover conditional superpolies. Second, by combining numeric mapping with monomial prediction techniques, we propose an automated cube search algorithm that is capable of generating a large number of good cubes for attacks. Finally, we develop two kinds of testing methods, which are used to efficiently extract substantial key information from large-scale equation systems.
To illustrate the power of our techniques, we apply them to Trivium. As a result, for 840 rounds of Trivium, a practical key recovery attack is mounted with complexity below $2^{55}$ and a success rate 77.8\%. For 845 rounds, we present a practical key recovery attack with complexity below $2^{56}$ and a success rate 98.1\% for $2^{80} \times 59.1\%$ keys. For 855 rounds, we present a theoretical weak-key recovery attack for $2^{74}$ keys. To the best of our knowledge, these are the best practical and theoretical attacks on Trivium. The improvements in the number of rounds reached are 13 for practical attacks and 4 for theoretical attacks, respectively.

item.title: Causal Awareness in End-to-End Encrypted Group Messaging
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2459
Authors: Joseph Jaeger, Akshaya Kumar, Igors Stepanovs
Summary: Chats do not always unfold in a single clear order. Two users may send messages before information about either message reaches the other sender. Such messages are concurrent, but most instant messengers provide no way for users to recognize this relationship. Chen and Fischlin (Eurocrypt 2024) studied this limitation in the two-user setting, showing that Signal does not expose enough information to recover the context in which a message was sent; they proposed a fix. We study group chats, where a user may need to reason about ordering and concurrency among other users' messages. This can become a security problem when network delays or adversarial interference cause an authentic message to be shown in a misleading context.
Event ordering is a classical problem; Lamport clocks and vector clocks are standard starting points. Secure messaging needs a different treatment because communication is asynchronous, bandwidth is limited, and added latency is undesirable. To address the problem under these constraints, we introduce causal awareness: the ability of a receiver to reconstruct a specified part of the causal context in which an accepted message was sent. Senders transmit records of what they have sent and received. Receivers verify these records and compare them with their own.
We develop a framework of correctness and security notions for causal awareness in group chats. Our definitions are parameterized by how much causal information receivers must recover. We give baseline constructions and prove their properties. We also introduce checkpoint-aided and server-aided variants of the framework and prove that, in each, our notions of correctness and integrity imply causal awareness. We discuss how causal information could be surfaced in a messenger's user interface.

item.title: Master-Key Recovery from Internal Activation Leakage in ReLU Realizations of Camellia
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2458
Authors: Kwangjo Kim
Summary: This paper investigates functional correctness and masterkey reconstruction in explicitly constructed rectified linear unit (ReLU) implementations of Camellia-128, Camellia-192, and Camellia-256. Exact neural realizations of Boolean gates, S-box selectors, and bit permutations provide a framework for reproducing Camellia on binary inputs. We present a component-wise correctness argument and report known-answer-test agreement for Camellia-128. We then analyze how selected whitening and round-key quantities determine the external master key through public key-schedule identities. Inverse rotations of suitable subkey pairs recover the required key components, whereas prewhitening-key recovery alone is insufficient for complete reconstruction of the longer keys. Under explicitly constructed synthetic internal-oracle access, symmetric real-valued perturbations identify target subkey bits, requiring 128 and 256 query pairs for the coordinate-wise Camellia-128 and Camellia-256 procedures, respectively. A separate Camellia-192 experiment validates deterministic key-schedule inversion under direct access to DNN-generated round keys. Across 1,000 independently sampled master keys per variant, all three procedures achieved exact recovery in every trial, yielding 3,000 successful recoveries out of 3,000 trials, with zero recovery failures and no Camellia-192 complement-consistency failures. These results validate conditional master-key reconstruction under the specified internal-access models and highlight the distinction between binary functional correctness and security under stronger access assumptions. They do not establish plaintext/ciphertext-only attacks against standard Camellia.

item.title: On Secure Sorting and Its Application to Privacy-Preserving Graph Pattern Matching
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2457
Authors: Marcel Keller
Summary: Sorting in secure computation has been studied almost as long as there have been implementations of multi-party computation (Wang et al., AsiaCCS'10). More recent advances include completely secure implementations (revealing nothing other than the list size) that have used Quicksort (Araki et al., CCS'21) and radix sort (Asharov et al., CCS'22). For the first time, we extensively compare the two variants across a range of parameters and for both honest- and dishonest-majority computation. We then apply secure sorting to improve sparse matrix multiplication without oblivious RAM based on recent work by Damie et al. (CODASPY'26). Our main contribution here is to produce an output in the same format as the inputs to the multiplication. This is needed for repeated multiplication of graph adjacency matrices, which we use to find cycles in graphs. Such cycles have been associated with money laundering, and this also applies to another graph pattern dubbed scatter-gather, which we can detect with the same approach. Our work therefore can be applied to privacy-preserving anti-money laundering detection.

item.title: On the Expected Number of Iterations in ML-DSA Signing: A Complete Accounting of the Rejection Conditions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2456
Authors: Kris Kwiatkowski
Summary: FIPS 204 Table 1 gives the expected number of iterations of the ML-DSA signing loop (ML-DSA.Sign_internal, Algorithm 7), citing CRYSTALS-Dilithium Equation (5). That equation covers only the validity checks on line 23 ($\lVert z \rVert_\infty$ and $\lVert r_0 \rVert_\infty$) and omits the two encoding-correctness checks on line 28 ($\lVert c \cdot t_0 \rVert_\infty$ and the hint weight), a scoping distinction the Dilithium specification states explicitly and FIPS 204 does not reproduce. We give a complete accounting of all four conditions. The $z$ check on line 23 is computed exactly by counting; the $c \cdot t_0$ term follows a closed-form Irwin-Hall tail, restating a peer-reviewed result by Yan, Luo and Wang; the hint-weight term's per-coefficient probability, conditioned on line 23 having passed, does have a closed form, but the tail of the sum over $256k$ such coefficients does not, since their probabilities are unequal, random, and correlated with each other, so we give the conditioned per-coefficient probability in closed form and estimate its tail by Monte Carlo. The corrected expected iteration counts are 4.36, 5.14 and 3.91 for ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87, matching a real end-to-end measurement to within 0.14% and already reflected in NIST's own errata to FIPS 204.

item.title: CUTS: Chained Uniform-sum Tree Signatures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2455
Authors: Jamie Judd, Louis Tajan, Conor Deegan, Furkan Akal
Summary: Stateful hash-based signatures fail badly when a one-time key signs twice, as happens when the signer's state is lost or rolled back. We study what a second signature reveals in a broad class of hash-based schemes whose key is a tree of hash chains. In this class, a message selects a set of tree nodes that covers every leaf exactly once, together with a position on the chain of each selected node, and the signature reveals the chain values at those positions. For the whole class, we prove that the values derivable from several signatures are exactly the union of those derivable from each signature alone, and we bound forgery after $b$ signatures in the classical random-oracle model by a combinatorial coverage exponent $\lambda_b$, also when the signer grinds a counter. We then present CUTS (Chained Uniform-sum Tree Signatures), a member of the class built on one binary tree, in which both the selected nodes and their chain positions depend on the message, with the positions summing to a fixed value $S$. Signature length and verification cost are fixed by the parameters and do not depend on the tree height. For CUTS, we compute the two-use coverage exactly as one coefficient of a polynomial and derive deterministic lower bounds on $\lambda_2$; one parameter set with 1 424-byte signatures has $\lambda_2\ge128.6$. A counter variant, CUTS+C, trades a short counter and extra signing work for a proven grinding gain of $g$ bits in the coverage term.

item.title: Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing: Below Half Threshold Rate
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2454
Authors: Hai H. Nguyen
Summary: We study the local leakage resilience of Shamir secret sharing, where an adversary leaks a bounded number of bits from every share. For $n$ parties and reconstruction threshold $k$ over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p>n$, we prove the following.
(1) There is an absolute constant $c_{\mathrm{bh}}<1/2$ such that, for $k\ge c_{\mathrm{bh}}n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to arbitrary one-bit leakage from every share. The best previous threshold was $0.668n$.
(2) For every fixed $0<\delta<1/2$ and $k\ge(1/2+\delta)n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to $\left\lfloor\frac{\delta}{24}\log_2 n\right\rfloor$ bits of arbitrary local leakage per share. By a recent attack, this number of bits is optimal up to a constant factor depending on $\delta$.
(3) For every fixed threshold rate $c>0$ and $k\ge cn$, Shamir sharing is resilient to quadratic-residue leakage and to almost all local leakage functions of up to $\eta_c\log_2 p$ bits, for a constant $\eta_c>0$.
All three results follow from one analytic framework, which we develop for generalized Reed--Solomon codes: local leakage from a uniform codeword is statistically close to the same leakage from independent uniform field elements. The framework expresses the leakage distance as the norm of a function on the leakage outputs. The Efron--Stein decomposition splits this function into orthogonal components indexed by supports of dual codewords. Two tools bound the components: list recovery of the dual code, which is ordinary list decoding for one-bit leakage, and a generalized von Neumann inequality for MDS systems of linear forms that retains linearly many Gowers norms. The first tool gives the result above half, the second gives the constant-rate result, and applying both to different ranges of supports in the same decomposition gives the result below half.

item.title: Revisiting Witness-Succinct UC-lifting Compilers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2453
Authors: Davide Li Calsi, Luigi Russo, Dominique Schröder, Federico Valbusa
Summary: Zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (zkSNARKs) are increasingly used within larger cryptographic protocols, making security under composition essential. Generic compilation to Universal Composability (UC) requires straight-line, black-box extraction while preserving succinctness and controlling prover cost.
We introduce verifiable reconstructible straightline codes (VRSCs), a primitive that separates public hiding, transcript-based reconstruction, binding, and proof non-rerandomizability. This abstraction exposes a missing security requirement in the witness-succinct UC compiler of Ganesh et al. (EUROCRYPT 2023). Permuting previously revealed evaluation openings produces a fresh accepting proof with non-negligible probability without violating non-extrapolation, invalidating the claimed simulation argument. Proof non-rerandomizability captures this attack at the certificate level. Our construction prevents transfers between repetitions through verifier-enforced disjoint evaluation domains.
We formulate a generic UC lifting theorem in terms of VRSCs and give a pairing-based instantiation using a Fischlin-style search over authenticated codeword symbols. Structured Reed--Solomon encoding and jointly computed KZG openings reduce certificate-generation work from quadratic to \(O_{\lambda}(n\log n)\), where \(n\) is the witness size. Only a linear-time encoding check enters the underlying SNARK circuit. To our knowledge, this is the first generic UC lifting compiler that simultaneously achieves quasi-linear prover overhead and constant additional proof size and verification work with respect to the witness size.

item.title: Genericity in multivariate cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2452
Authors: Simon Abelard, Pierre Pébereau, Mohab Safey El Din
Summary: The results in this paper establish the genericity of some properties of the ideals and varieties generated by UOV public keys, in particular the equidimensionality of the UOV varieties and the radicality of public key ideals. These genericity results justify the various regularity assumptions that are made on polynomial systems of equations arising in the cryptanalysis of UOV and its variants. We also provide examples in the recent literature showing how genericity questions arise in crypt- analysis and why genericity should be taken into consideration when de- signing cryptographic schemes. Lastly, we perform a retrospective study of various cryptographic schemes through the viewangle of genericity. We identify several cases in which non-genericity led to the cryptanaly- sis of the scheme, but also provide a counter-example of a scheme whose non-genericity does not seem easy to exploit.

item.title: Extended biprojective APN functions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2451
Authors: Nadiia Ichanska, Nikolay Kaleyski
Summary: Almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions provide optimal resistance to differential cryptanalysis in characteristic two, and constructing new infinite families inequivalent to the known ones remains an important problem in the study of cryptographic functions. We introduce extended biprojective functions, obtained by augmenting biprojective polynomials with truncated trace terms, and establish a new infinite family of quadratic APN functions. To investigate these constructions, we develop an efficient APN test based on the ranks of binary matrices and employ it in exhaustive searches in dimensions up to 28. Using ortho-derivative differential spectra to distinguish CCZ-equivalence classes, we identify APN functions inequivalent to known families and uncover a systematic pattern across dimensions, leading to conjectures on further infinite families of quadratic APN functions.

item.title: Modulus Operandi: Round-Optimal Modulus Conversion for MPC and Threshold FHE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2450
Authors: Ivan Damgård, Sebastian Hasler, Sebastian Kolby, Stanislas Pawlak
Summary: In secure multiparty computation (MPC), modulus conversion turns a sharing of a value $x$ modulo $q$ into a sharing of the same value modulo $t$, without leaking anything about $x$. One important application of modulus conversion is in threshold decryption for lattice-based cryptosystems, where a sharing modulo the ciphertext modulus has to be moved to the plaintext modulus before it can be opened. The most efficient protocols so far (Damgård et al., Asiacrypt 2026) are in the preprocessing model, assume $x$ is bounded away from $q$ by a constant factor and take two rounds for a prime target modulus, three rounds for arbitrary moduli, and one round when all moduli are 2-powers. We improve upon this by constructing three new modulus conversion protocols in the preprocessing model:
- Our first conversion protocol takes a single round for arbitrary moduli, consisting of just one opening. - Our second conversion protocol is a variant of the first protocol, where in the preprocessing most of the secure multiplications are replaced by private inputs, which are checked in a batch using fully linear interactive oracle proofs (FLIOPs). This makes the preprocessing cheaper (amortized over a batch of conversions) when the number $N$ of parties is small. This comes at the cost of making the bound on $x$ a factor $N$ stronger. - Our third conversion protocol avoids the bound on $x$ altogether but takes two rounds.
All our protocols are stated in the arithmetic black box (ABB) model, so they can run on top of a wide variety of MPC protocols, inheriting their corruption threshold and security model.
To allow the third conversion protocol to run in two rounds, we construct the first one-round comparison protocol in the ABB model for comparing a bitwise shared $n$-bit value against a public threshold with polynomial-size preprocessing. Concretely, the preprocessing size is $\mathcal O(n^2)$ in general, and $\mathcal O(n^2 / \log n)$ in our case where the secret value is fixed in preprocessing.
We also construct constant-round ABB protocols without preprocessing for computing symmetric functions and comparisons of values shared bitwise modulo powers of arbitrary primes (e.g., $2^k$), at communication quasi-linear in the number of input bits. Previously, this required either a sufficiently large prime or polynomially larger communication.
Finally, we give an impossibility result for non-interactive modulus conversion, demonstrating that a single round is optimal: unless $t$ divides $q$, every non-interactive conversion for inputs $x < q/\beta$ is incorrect with probability at least $\approx 1/(4\beta)$.

item.title: Optimal Threshold Implementations of all bijective 4-bit S-boxes and new Infinite Families
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2449
Authors: Enrico Piccione, Yevhen Perehuda, Gregor Leander, Patrick Felke
Summary: Threshold implementations (TIs) are now an established class of side-channel countermeasures. Their underlying idea is simple and compelling: under mild, practical assumptions, they provide protection against glitches and allow composability. Yet our understanding of one-stage TIs with a minimal number of shares remains limited, both for cryptographically relevant families—particularly power functions—and for concrete small functions. In particular, until now, except for Feistel-constructions, no optimal TI had been found for families of mathematically well-structured and cryptographically non-trivial functions, especially power functions. In small dimensions, many functions - particularly cryptographically interesting ones — were not known to admit an optimal TI. This was especially true for the 4-bit S-boxes frequently used in practical lightweight ciphers. Optimal refers to share-optimal, direct one-stage, uniform, first-order TI. Here, we introduce new families of TIs, including the first infinite families of cryptographically nontrivial power permutations. Moreover, every four-bit permutation of algebraic degree t admits a direct, uniform TI with t+1 shares and no fresh randomness. Those results prove several previous conjectures and claims wrong. Since such permutations are widely used in symmetric ciphers, our constructions offer new implementation options.
$\textbf{Note:}$ The threshold implementations presented in this paper are available at: https://github.com/enripicc/Optimal-Threshold-Implementations-for-3-4-and-5-bits-permutations

item.title: Breaking First-Order Masked Kyber with Belief Propagation Alone
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2448
Authors: Vahid Jahandideh, Lejla Batina
Summary: We recover the long-term key of a first-order masked Kyber768 implementation on an ARM Cortex-M4 from about 2200 decapsulation power traces, using only authentic ciphertexts that pass ciphertext-validity checks. The secret is freshly shared before every decapsulation, and the attack combines weak second-order leakage from both shares. Under the evaluated leakage model, even exact Hamming weights of both shares provide about 97% less mutual information about a decryption-noise coefficient than the exact Hamming weight of the unmasked coefficient. A profiled neural network estimates Hamming-weight distributions for the two arithmetic shares of each noisy message coefficient. We combine these distributions into likelihoods on the decryption noise, which is a known affine function of the secret and the public-key error. A belief-propagation (BP) solver accumulates these likelihoods across traces, preserving their non-Gaussian shapes while approximating the aggregate interference from other key coordinates by a Gaussian. An Onsager correction from approximate message passing corrects for feedback between each factor and the current beliefs. The solver recovers all 1536 secret and error coefficients without lattice reduction. At the evaluated trace budgets, least squares performs no better than the all-zero estimate, and a greedy inequality solver fails even with exact Hamming weights. The evaluated primal-lattice cascade does not reduce the trace requirement: below BP's recovery threshold, its output remains too diffuse to enable practical lattice recovery. At 2000 traces, BP-derived hints lower the estimated BKZ block size from 624 to 505, leaving the lattice attack impractical.

item.title: A methodology to derive security specifications for complex electronic systems
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2447
Authors: Sylvain Guilley, Ritu Ranjan Shrivstwa, Ville Yli-Mäyry
Summary: Modern electronic systems are becoming increas- ingly complex and must satisfy demanding performance, power, and area (PPA) constraints. Consider for instance artificial intelligence chips, aiming at datacenters running LLMs or at automotive perception, which manipulate massive data streams. Beyond performance considerations, these systems must also provide increasingly strong security and dependability guaran- tees. Indeed, when electronic systems are based on chiplets, for instance, the supply chain gets longer and therefore brings a larger number of threats. Also, those systems are very versatile, in that they can run varied multi-tenant applications. Therefore, defining what security features are required in this context with numerous stakes is not trivial. Existing scholarly research is very relevant when the security problem is well defined. The resulting scientific papers accord- ingly dig very deep: this modus operandi has proved productive in exploring new problems, and actually allowed to come up with innovative solutions. For instance, in the field of side-channel attacks, varied mitigations alongside with metrics to evaluate them have been devised. Increasing sophistication resulted from this research, as external considerations have been injected into the problem (typically, aspects such as attack order, impact of combinatorial glitches, etc.). Therefore, we face today the question of selecting the most suitable technology amongst the proliferation of state-of-the-art techniques. In addition, in complex systems, we encounter another prob- lem, namely that of defining the security problem(s). A fruitful approach in this respect is a risk based approach. Specifically, the application of a risk-oriented methodology allows to reason on the security rationale. It proceeds as follows. First, the system missions are listed. Then for each of them, the necessary assets are deduced. A threat analysis allows to identify how assets are threatened, and eventually, security requirements can be enunciated. At this stage, the task of matching relevant countermeasures becomes straightforward. This paper illustrates the methodology by deriving security specifications for datacenter and automotive chiplets. The considered missions are (secure) provisioning, trimming, debugging, booting, and remote attestation.

item.title: Chosen Ciphertext and Trapdoor Secure Public Key Authenticated Encryption with Keyword Search
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2446
Authors: Tomoki Mori, Keita Emura
Summary: For public-key encryption with keyword search (PEKS), chosen-ciphertext attack (CCA) security has been studied in settings where an adversary is allowed to access the test oracle. Notably, the CHK transformation (Canetti, Halevi, and Katz, EUROCRYPT 2004) does not yield CCA-secure PEKS. To address this limitation, Abdalla, Bellare, and Neven (TCC 2010/JoC 2018) proposed a generic construction of CCA-secure PEKS from CCA-secure anonymous and weakly robust identity-based encryption. However, CCA security alone is insufficient to resist keyword-guessing attacks (KGAs) arising from trapdoor leakage in PEKS. To mitigate KGAs, public-key authenticated encryption with keyword search (PAEKS) has been studied. In particular, Li and Boyen (IACR CiC 2024) proposed a generic construction of PAEKS. In this paper, we propose a generic transformation that converts a PAEKS scheme into a CCTA-secure one, where CCTA denotes security against chosen-ciphertext and trapdoor attacks. Our transformation can be viewed as a variant of the CHK transformation. The key observation is that, unlike in PEKS, the receiver in PAEKS identifies and specifies the sender when generating a trapdoor, enabling keywords to be used as tags. The transformation directly upgrades PAEKS instantiations obtained via the Li-Boyen generic construction under various assumptions to CCTA-secure schemes. As a result, we obtain the first fully CCTA-secure PAEKS schemes from both pairings and lattices. As an additional benefit, the transformation improves search efficiency. By leveraging verification keys embedded in ciphertexts and trapdoors, sender-receiver matching can be performed without cryptographic computation, for example, by using hash tables. Consequently, for a trapdoor associated with a particular sender, the search complexity measured in cryptographic operations becomes independent of the number of senders and is essentially the same as that of PEKS. Although improving efficiency is not the primary goal of the transformation, this benefit is of independent interest.

item.title: A Black-Box Compiler from Static to Dynamic SNARKs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2445
Authors: Anubhav Baweja, Charalampos Papamanthou
Summary: Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge (SNARKs) for NP allow a prover to prove knowledge of a witness of an NP relation to a verifier with a short proof. The primary goal of a (static) SNARK is to make verification cheap: the proof should be short, and the verifier's work should be minimal. However, recent work has also focused on making SNARKs more prover-efficient: cheap verification should ideally not come at the cost of large prover overhead. One avenue for achieving prover efficiency is via Dynamic SNARKs, which allow a prover to efficiently update the proof when the witness is updated. For example, one may use a SNARK to issue a proof of a query being performed correctly on a database, and then issue a new proof of the query once the database is updated. If these updates are small compared to the size of the witness (only a single entry of a large database is updated), then the prover should ideally be able to use the old proof to generate a new proof in time proportional to the distance between the old and the new witness.
While some constructions of dynamic SNARKs for NP have been recently proposed by Wang et al. [Eurocrypt 2026] and Zhang et al. [Eurocrypt 2026], they have many limitations, such as lack of post-quantum security, dependence on a setup by a trusted third-party, and poor asymptotic and concrete efficiency. In this work, we present a compiler for constructing a dynamic SNARK for Plonkish constraints (which capture arbitrary NP computations) by using a static SNARK for NP and a vector commitment scheme as black boxes. When instantiated with a state-of-the-art hash-based SNARK and Merkle trees, the compiler yields a dynamic SNARK that is post-quantum secure in the QROM, has a transparent setup, and achieves $O(n)$ initial prover time and $O(k \log^2 n)$ update prover time, with succinct proofs and verification, where $k$ is the Hamming distance between the old and new instance-witness pairs. Our Ligerito-based implementation achieves cumulative prover speedups of $147\times$ and $11.7\times$ over a static HyperPlonk baseline for 10,000 successive one-gate updates and 1,000 successive 128-gate updates, respectively, on a $2^{23}$-gate circuit, including the full dynamic initialization cost.

item.title: Extending the Schur--Macaulay Framework for UOV Attacks via Truncated Polynomial Algebras
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2444
Authors: Peigen Li, Siyong Tao
Summary: Building on the wedge-attack framework of Ding, Li, and Tao , we reformulate the Schur-Macaulay matrix approach of Merz and Ran in polynomial terms and develop a unified treatment using truncated polynomial algebras over fields of positive characteristic $p$. By working in $p$-truncated polynomial algebras, our formulation applies to the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) problem over arbitrary finite fields. Divided powers and transfer relations yield additional public relations within the ideal-inclusion framework, leading to quotient-dimension criteria for recovering graded components of the hidden oil-space ideal. As an application, we analyze the third-round QR-UOV parameter sets and obtain lower estimates of attack complexity for some of them.

item.title: Worst-Case Hardness for Succinct and Decomposed Learning with Errors
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2443
Authors: Damiano Abram, Gal Arnon, Valerio Cini, Paul Lou, Giulio Malavolta, Lawrence Roy
Summary: The succinct LWE (CRYPTO~'24) and decomposed LWE (CRYPTO~'25) assumptions are two recently introduced variants of the celebrated LWE problem, known to imply the existence of numerous new cryptographic primitives. Yet, the hardness of these problems has thus far remained poorly understood, since there is no known reduction to LWE.
In this work, we study these lattice problems from a foundational perspective. Our main technical contribution is a worst-case-to-average-case reduction from \emph{superlattice SVP} (SuperSVP) to succinct SIS. We introduce SuperSVP as a variant of SVP for general lattices in which the solver is additionally given, as a hint, a short basis for a related superlattice. Combining this result with our quantum reduction from succinct SIS to succinct LWE, which is an analog of Regev's SIS-to-LWE reduction, and with our search-to-decision reduction establishes worst-case hardness for succinct LWE. Finally, we show that succinct and decomposed LWE are equivalent, extending this conclusion to decomposed LWE.
Overall, our work places succinct and decomposed LWE on firmer theoretical ground and, as a direct consequence, establishes the \emph{worst-case} hardness of a variety of cryptographic primitives, known to be implied by these assumptions.

item.title: Faster generic CCA secure KEM transformation using encrypt-then-MAC
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2442
Authors: Ganyu Xu, Kalikinkar Mandal, Guang Gong
Summary: ML-KEM is a lattice-based IND-CCA secure key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) standardized by NIST in FIPS 203. ML-KEM achieves chosen-ciphertext security by applying the Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) transformation to an IND-CPA secure public key encryption (PKE) scheme. The FO transformation uses de-randomization and re-encryption to ensure ciphertext non-malleability, but because ML-KEM's underlying PKE encryption subroutine is slower than the decryption subroutine, ML-KEM's decapsulation performance is dominated by re-encryption. In this paper, we revisit the ``encrypt-then-MAC'' paradigm as a generic KEM transformation: the PKE ciphertext is authenticated by a message authentication code (MAC) whose key is derived from the PKE plaintext. We prove that the transformation achieves IND-CCA security in the random oracle model when the underlying PKE is one-way under plaintext-checking attack (OW-PCA), and we introduce a fine-grained security notion, one-wayness under $q$-bounded plaintext-checking attack (OW-$q$PCA), under which the transformation achieves IND-$q$CCA security. In contrast to the tag-based IND-1CCA transformations of Huguenin-Dumittan and Vaudenay (Eurocrypt 2022), whose tag is a random-oracle hash of the plaintext and the entire ciphertext, our transformation applies the random oracle only to the short PKE plaintext, while the long ciphertext is processed by a standard-model MAC that needs only to be one-time existentially unforgeable. We present ML-KEM-EtM, an IND-$q$CCA secure KEM derived from applying the encrypt-then-MAC transformation to the PKE subroutines of ML-KEM, and McElieceEtM, an instantiation with Classic McEliece that achieves full IND-CCA security under the conjectured OW-PCA security of its Niederreiter PKE. We implement ML-KEM-EtM with a wide selection of MACs including Poly1305, GMAC, CMAC, and KMAC256. At the cost of minimal increase in encapsulation CPU cycle count and ciphertext size, ML-KEM-EtM achieves a substantial reduction of the decapsulation CPU cycle count.

item.title: Nobody Will Read the Lean: A Case for High-Level Cryptographic Languages
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2441
Authors: Nadim Kobeissi
Summary: In September 2026, an AI produced a Lean proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in eleven days, and AI provers have started on cryptography. Within a few years, an AI may hand you a machine-checked proof that Signal is secure. You won't need to read it, because Lean will have checked every step. What Lean can't check is whether the theorem says what you think it says. That depends on its definitions, which the AI will also have written at length for that one proof. This already happens. A Lean library's security theorem for Schnorr signatures passed the checker, yet as written it held for every adversary and so promised nothing.
When proofs are cheap, the scarce resource is a person who can read what was proved. I argue that we should build high-level cryptographic languages for that person. A protocol's owners should write its model themselves, short enough for one or two people to read. Every claim the language makes should rest on a checked theorem. And definitions of protocol goals such as forward secrecy should be built in: a small set, versioned and agreed in public the way we agree on AES, so that a property's name means the same thing in every report. Today it may not: on a one-page Verifpal model, two of five verdicts would flip under other standard definitions, with neither answer wrong. Agreeing on definitions will take years of public argument that better provers can't shorten, so we should start now.

item.title: Staggered Instruction-Fetch Duplication: A Lightweight Processor-Level Countermeasure Against Fault Injection
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2440
Authors: Shoei Nashimoto, Naoya Okada, Yuichiro Murachi
Summary: Fault attacks exploit transient hardware faults to bypass software-level security checks in embedded processors. Processor-level redundancy can detect such faults, but duplicating the whole processor is costly for resource-constrained devices. This paper proposes Staggered Instruction-Fetch Duplication (SIFD), a lightweight processor-level countermeasure based on instruction-fetch redundancy. SIFD fetches each instruction twice in consecutive cycles, while fetching two different instructions in every fetch cycle. This staggered schedule detects inconsistent fetch results without full processor duplication, compiler support, or cryptographic hardware. We implement SIFD on a custom RV32I processor and evaluate it on an Artix-7 FPGA using clock fault injection (CFI) and electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI). SIFD increases slice utilization by 15.0% and execution time by 16.3%. It reduces the attack success rate from 0.86% to below 0.01% under CFI and from 0.32% to 0.13% under EMFI. It also detects 73.18% of CFI attempts and 11.44% of EMFI attempts. These results indicate that SIFD can convert many fault effects into explicit detections and reduce successful fault-injection outcomes, especially under CFI.

item.title: Efficient Vectorized Implementation of MQOM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2439
Authors: David Santos, Julio López, Francisco Rodríguez-Henríquez
Summary: Post-quantum signature schemes require efficient implementations to be viable in practice. MQOM, a third-round candidate in NIST’s additional call for digital signatures, is a promising target for SIMD optimization. This work leverages a transpose-enabled paired-matrix trick to develop a vectorized implementation of MQOM v2.1, corresponding to the Round-2 specification, with reduced wasted SIMD work and memory traffic. We evaluate MQOM v2.1 on Arm NEON, x86 AVX2, and x86 AVX-512, covering key generation, signing, verification, and memory; peak dynamic memory falls by up to 39.43%. We also include supplementary MQOM v3 experiments to assess how the matrix-layout optimization transfers to the Round-3 code.

item.title: Censorship Resistance in Credential Systems and Application to the EUDI Wallet
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2438
Authors: Pierpaolo Della Monica, Ivan Visconti, Andrea Vitaletti, Marco Zecchini
Summary: Privacy-preserving credential systems typically focus on data protection during the presentation phase, overlooking potential privacy threats during issuance. A malicious issuer could use the non-minimal information it obtains to deny issuance selectively. Such a denial, going beyond the eligibility policy, is a form of censorship. In this work, we revisit the security of anonymous credential systems to protect users from malicious issuers during credential issuance. We first highlight the limitations of existing definitions and introduce a security model capturing censorship resistance. Next, we present a round-optimal (i.e., one message per party) construction built from blind signatures and specifically tailored for selective disclosure in the presentation phase. Finally, we present CRACS, an instantiation of our construction, deployable within the European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDIW) framework. CRACS improves on the current reference implementation of the EUDIW, maintaining selective disclosure and yielding unlinkability between presentation and issuance sessions in addition to censorship resistance. Unlike prior work, CRACS confines advanced cryptography to issuance, leaving secure elements, the standardized credential formats, signature schemes, and presentation mechanisms untouched. It can therefore be deployed incrementally alongside current EUDIW implementations, issuer by issuer and user by user, with no change for verifiers.

item.title: Confidential Error-Correcting Codes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2437
Authors: Tianrui Wang, Anyu Wang, Tianshuo Cong, Delong Ran, Xiaoyun Wang
Summary: We introduce Confidential Error-correcting Codes (CECs), a new cryptographic primitive that enables reliable decoding from perturbed codewords while preserving message confidentiality. We formalize this primitive through three security properties: confidentiality, robustness, and soundness. To realize this goal, we develop a general framework for constructing CECs based on a Randomness-Security Separation (RSS) structure, which first encodes a nonce to introduce randomness and then masks the encoded payload with a pseudorandom function. Based on our RSS framework, we instantiate CECs, called Conc-CEC, using concatenated Reed-Muller and Reed-Solomon codes. The resulting Conc-CEC admits provable guarantees for all three properties. Notably, compared to PRCs (CRYPTO'24), another recent cryptographic primitive with error-correcting capability, CECs achieve significantly stronger concrete security guarantees under practical parameter settings. As a primary application of CECs, we further present CECMark, a watermarking scheme for AI-generated images. Our experiments on real-world generative image models show that CECMark consistently outperforms state-of-the-art watermarking methods, including Gaussian Shading (CVPR'24), PRCMark (ICLR'25), and T2SMark (NeurIPS'25). In particular, CECMark achieves higher robustness across all 56 evaluated perturbations and ensures a false positive rate below $10^{-5}$ without introducing side effects. Taken together, our work lays a novel cryptographic foundation for trustworthy watermarking schemes that, for the first time, unify provable security guarantees with strong practical reliability.

item.title: Threshold BARGs with Statistical Soundness: Weighted Threshold Encryption without Obfuscation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2436
Authors: Shafik Nassar, Brent Waters, David J. Wu
Summary: Non-interactive batch arguments (BARGs) for $\mathsf{NP}$ enable proving the validity of $k$ $\mathsf{NP}$ statements with a proof whose size is independent of $k$. Threshold BARGs are a natural generalization that enables proving that at least $t$ out of $k$ statements are valid. Unfortunately, existing threshold BARG constructions have the drawback that the size of the common reference string (CRS) grows polynomially with $k$. This is the case even when the statements have a short description (e.g., when considering index languages). Moreover, other than constructions based on indistinguishability obfuscation ($i\mathcal{O}$), prior constructions could only achieve computational soundness.
In this work, we construct the first threshold BARG with statistical soundness for an expressive class of trapdoor threshold languages from either circular-secure fully homomorphic encryption or from witness encryption in combination with the learning with errors assumption. Moreover and importantly for our applications, the size of the CRS only scales polylogarithmically with $k$.
Next, we combine our threshold BARG with a new technique for sampling pseudorandom permutations in order to build weighted threshold signatures with a statistical unforgeability guarantee. Then, in combination with witness encryption, we obtain a weighted threshold encryption scheme that supports $\lambda$-bit weights. Decryption is entirely non-interactive in our setting. Previously, such a scheme was only known from $i\mathcal{O}$. If we additionally work in the random oracle model, then we obtain a weighted threshold encryption scheme that supports arbitrary weights with silent setup. In the silent setup model, users choose their own public/secret keys and no longer need to rely on a central authority to generate and issue decryption keys.

item.title: TenseUp: Doubly-Efficient Lookup Arguments from Tensor Codes and Applications to Dynamic SNARKs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2435
Authors: Christodoulos Pappas, Pariya Akhiani, Yupeng Zhang, Dimitrios Papadopoulos
Summary: Doubly-Efficient Lookup Arguments are specialized argument systems that enable succinctly proving the correctness of a batch of $k$ lookup accesses to a large table $\textbf{x}$ in time proportional to $k$ and sublinear in $|\textbf{x}|$. All existing such schemes suffer from one of the following limitations. Either they rely on elliptic-curve-based assumptions for their security, hence they are not secure against quantum adversaries, or are rather impractical, as they rely on algorithms for fast polynomial evaluations (that are mostly of theoretical interest), or operate over fields of small characteristic---making them incompatible with most modern argument systems. In this work, we use tensor codes to construct transparent and post-quantum secure updatable doubly-efficient lookup arguments that asymptotically outperform all existing schemes with the same properties, in terms of prover time and/or preprocessing. By further optimizing this approach for a specific type of two-dimensional tensor codes, we build TenseUp, a concretely efficient lookup argument that, as shown in our experiments, has comparable or even better performance than state-of-the-art non-post-quantum secure prior doubly-efficient lookup arguments. As an independent contribution, we propose a general-purpose compiler for building dynamic SNARKs from any ``static'' SNARK, via judicious use of updatable doubly efficient lookup arguments to store and access witness updates. Applying our compiler with different SNARKs and lookup arguments can lead to different novel results; e.g., combining a hash-based SNARK with our lookup arguments yields the first transparent and post-quantum secure dynamic SNARK.

item.title: Witness-Succinct UC-Secure SNARKs with Weaker Trust Assumptions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2434
Authors: Nahid Roustaeifar, Maryam Zarezadeh, Neel Mehendale, Behzad Abdolmaleki, Mahshid Delavar, Stefan Köpsell
Summary: Zero-knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge (zkSNARKs) are foundational cryptographic primitives enabling privacy-preserving and verifiable computation. However, most existing zkSNARK constructions rely on strong trust assumptions—typically a fully trusted setup—which undermines their applicability in adversarial or decentralized environments. Although transparent zkSNARKs remove this assumption, they typically do not satisfy strong composability guarantees such as Universal Composability (UC).
In this work, we present the first framework for constructing UC-secure zkSNARKs under weaker trust assumptions, based on a new primitive called Key-Updatable Polynomial Commitments (KU-pCom). This primitive enables publicly verifiable commitment-key updates, requiring only one honest update rather than a fully trusted setup. Our compiler transforms any Simulation-Extractable zkSNARK into a UC-secure variant by composing it with a KU-pCom scheme. We instantiate our framework in two settings: (1) using the structured, trusted setup of the KZG commitment scheme, and (2) an instantiation based on the lattice-based commitment scheme of Hwang et al. (Crypto 2024). We implement both instantiations and provide an end-to-end benchmark of UC-secure zkSNARKs with succinctness. Compared to prior UC-secure NIZKs that sacrifice succinctness (e.g., Abdolmaleki et al., CSF 2024), our work demonstrates that UC security, succinctness, and practical efficiency can be simultaneously achieved, establishing a new foundation for succinct, composable proof systems under weaker trust assumptions.

item.title: Succinct Arguments with (almost) Minimal Time and Space Overheads from Symmetric-Key Primitives
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2433
Authors: Alexander R. Block, Caleb Geren, Pratik Soni
Summary: We construct public-coin, succinct, zero-knowledge interactive arguments for NP relations decided by time-$T$, space-$S$ random-access machines. Assuming the existence of collision-resistant hash functions, our arguments give a frontier of tradeoffs between prover time and space, and proof size. We follow the streaming PIOP+PCS framework of Block et al. (TCC 2020, CRYPTO 2021), reducing the problem of constructing time- and space-efficient arguments to time- and space-efficient streaming multilinear polynomial commitment schemes (MLPCS).
We develop two code-based streaming MLPCS inspired by Brakedown (CRYPTO 2023) and BaseFold (CRYPTO 2024), implementing each scheme when additionally given succinct access to the underlying encoding matrices. We instantiate this framework assuming row-sparse, column-sparse, and Reed-Solomon encoders, then apply a generic PIOP + MLPCS compiler to obtain our (zero-knowledge) time- and space-efficient arguments. Finally, as all our protocols are public-coin, applying Fiat-Shamir yields time- and space-efficient (zk)SNARKs from symmetric-key primitives (i.e., collision-resistant hashing).
Our Brakedown-based constructions have \(O(\log T)\) rounds and \(\widetilde O(\sqrt T)\)-size proofs and verification time, with two complementary prover profiles: (i) \(\widetilde O(S)\) space (which is optimal) and \(\widetilde O(T^{3/2})\) time, and (ii) \(\widetilde O(T)\) time (nearly optimal) and \(\widetilde O(S+\sqrt T)\) space. Our BaseFold-based constructions achieve $\mathrm{polylog}(T)$ proof size and verification time with \(O(\log T)\) rounds. We again obtain two complementary prover profiles: (i) an encoder parameterized construction with \(\widetilde O(T+T_{\mathrm{Enc}})\) time and \(\widetilde O(S + S_{\mathrm{Enc}})\) space, where \(T_{\mathrm{Enc}}, S_{\mathrm{Enc}}\) are the running time and space of a streaming log-space encoder for a suitable linear code, and (ii) an unconditional sub-quadratic instantiation \(\widetilde O(T^{3/2})\) time and \(\widetilde O(S+\sqrt T)\) space.

item.title: Lattice Bingo: Asynchrony and One-Shot Adaptivity in Verifiable Secret Sharing via Erasure Code Commitments
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2432
Authors: Ittai Abraham, Aniket Kate, Aditi Partap, Ertem Nusret Tas
Summary: Asynchronous verifiable secret sharing (AVSS) allows a dealer to distribute a secret among parties while preserving privacy and consistent reconstruction, despite Byzantine faults and arbitrary message delays. It is a fundamental building block for Byzantine agreement, distributed key generation, and secure multiparty computation. Packed AVSS protocols share many secrets together to reduce communication per secret. The best known AVSS protocols achieve quadratic communication while sharing linearly many secrets. In particular, Bingo (Abraham et al., CRYPTO 2023) shares a batch of $\Theta(k)$ secrets among $k$ parties using $O(\lambda k^2)$ words of communication, while also achieving adaptive security, but relies on assumptions that are not post-quantum secure. Known post-quantum alternatives have higher worst-case communication for comparable batch sizes or require substantially larger batches to achieve linear amortized communication.
We present Lattice Bingo, a lattice-based packed AVSS protocol with quadratic communication and linear packing. For every constant $\epsilon>0$, it shares $\Theta(k)$ secrets among $k\geq(3+\epsilon)f$ parties, tolerates $f$ Byzantine parties, and uses $O(k^2\operatorname{poly}(\lambda))$ words of communication. It additionally achieves one-shot adaptive secrecy: the adversary may adaptively choose its corruption and reconstruction requests based on the public transcript observed so far, but must submit these requests together in a single batch.
Our main technical contribution is a commitment scheme for two-dimensional linear codes based on the PowerBASIS assumption. We combine PowerBASIS commitments with the linear code based secret sharing of Applebaum, Nir, and Pinkas, replacing the Reed–Solomon encoding and KZG commitments used in Bingo. Our commitment supports proof interpolation, enabling parties to recover missing shares and their opening proofs. It additionally achieves a notion that we call one-shot simulation hiding. Together, these properties allow us to adapt Bingo’s framework to obtain Lattice Bingo with the same efficiency and one-shot adaptive security.

item.title: Flying, Not Floating: Precise Fixed-Point Falcon on Embedded Processors
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2431
Authors: Stef Halmans, Amit Kumar, Tim Güneysu
Summary: The Falcon digital signature scheme, under standardization as FN-DSA, requires real-number arithmetic during signing, with its security dependent on numerical precision. Recently, De Almeida Braga et al. (CRYPTO 2026) showed that Falcon-512 can sign in 64.64 fixed-point arithmetic on 64-bit hosts. In this work, we present the first fixed-point FN-DSA signer for microcontrollers, using 32.64 arithmetic in constant-time Cortex-M4 assembly for Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024. Although a straightforward fixed-point implementation is less precise than double precision, our new techniques successfully restore precision. They keep reciprocals, inverse square roots and small constants wide and round once at the consumer. We evaluate them with known techniques on both arithmetics and both degrees. Our signer needs around $45\%$ fewer cycles than double-precision emulation for Falcon-512 Falcon-1024, and its measured precision supports $2^{99.7}$ $2^{96.7}$ queries per key, against $2^{61.5}$ $2^{58.7}$ for double precision and the target of $2^{64}$. Our $12$-byte words raise signing RAM from $59n$ to $83n$ bytes. We also show which implementation choices lift double-precision c-fn-dsa above $2^{64}$ while making it faster. We derive key generation bounds for Falcon-1024, accepting $72.3\%$ of keys where the Falcon-512 values accept $8.5\%$, and provide recommendations for the fixed-point FN-DSA that NIST plans.

item.title: Distinguishers for the Squeezing of the Alternating Sponge and Duet
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2430
Authors: Gaëtan Leurent, César Mathéus
Summary: Recently, the Institute of Commercial Cryptography Standards (ICCS) launched the Next Generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithm Program (NGCC), which includes a standardization process for cryptographic hash functions. In this note, we analyze the mode of operation of Duet, one of the hash-function candidates.
Duet is a permutation-based hash function directly inspired by the Alternating Sponge (ASP). Both constructions use two permutations on $b=r+c$ bits, split into an outer part of $r$ bits and an inner part of $c$ bits. We first present a distinguisher against ASP requiring $\mathcal{O}(2^r)$ permutation queries, which contradicts the claimed indifferentiability bound in a non-trivial parameter regime. We then introduce a distinguisher and a state-recovery attack against Duet. Both attacks require only a constant number of $h$-bit output blocks, with $h\leq c$, and $\mathcal{O}(2^{r+c-h})$ permutation queries. These attacks do not affect the claimed collision or preimage resistance, but they distinguish Duet's multi-block output from random, with consequences if Duet is used as a XOF or a KDF; state recovery also enables length extension.

item.title: Rapid mixing in superspecial isogeny graphs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2429
Authors: Maria Corte-Real Santos, Harun Kır, Olivier Taïbi, Benjamin Wesolowski
Summary: We prove expansion properties of superspecial isogeny graphs in dimension $g \geq 2$, including arbitrary level structure. In particular, we provide explicit bounds for the spectral gap, and a fine characterization of obstructions created by level structures (disconnectedness and periodicity). Without the level structure (the only case which was previously studied), our bounds dramatically improve the state of the art.
These isogenies in dimension greater than one have become increasingly important in isogeny-based cryptography, and previous works have already conjectured consequences of their expansion properties. We present several applications of our result: we transform conjectural predecessors into rigorous algorithms, and we give the first algorithm for computing endomorphism rings of superspecial principally polarized abelian varieties in arbitrary dimension, with complexity $\tilde O(p^{g-1})$.

item.title: Beyond-Birthday MAC Security for Encrypted Wegman-Carter and EWCDMD
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2428
Authors: Yuxiang Wang, Chun Guo, Sihuang Hu
Summary: At CRYPTO 2016, Cogliati and Seurin proposed EWCDM as a nonce-based MAC construction making two block cipher calls and one almost-XOR-universal (AXU) hash evaluation and achieving beyond-birthday-bound (BBB) security. They noticed that a simplified variant of EWCDM named Encrypted Wegman--Carter (EWC) admits a birthday distinguishing attack. Later, at CRYPTO 2017, Mennink and Neves proposed EWCDMD, the dual of EWCDM, as a new candidate BBB-secure MAC, but at EUROCRYPT 2020 Nandi proposed a birthday distinguishing attack against EWCDMD. However, the distinguishing attacks did not yield forgeries, and whether EWC and EWCDMD have BBB unforgeability (or MAC security) remains open.
We prove beyond-birthday unforgeability for EWC and EWCDMD and answer this long-standing open problem positively. Using an $n$-bit block cipher and an $O(2^{-n})$-AXU hash family, we prove that both constructions are secure up to $2^{5n/6}$ MAC queries and nearly $2^n$ verification queries, in the nonce-respecting setting.
To bypass the birthday distinguishing attacks, our proofs directly analyze forgery events using auxiliary experiments indexed by hash values and messages. For EWC, we additionally employ conditional permutation analysis and collision multiplicity bounds with KL divergence, whereas for EWCDMD we use Hellinger distance and Fourier analysis.

item.title: RM-KLPT: Algebraic Pathfinding for Superspecial Abelian Surfaces with Maximal Real Multiplication
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2427
Authors: Mingjie Chen, Thomas Decru, Péter Kutas, Mickaël Montessinos, Sebastian A. Spindler, Nicolas Swanson
Summary: The isogeny graphs of superspecial abelian surfaces with maximal real multiplication were first studied by Charles, Goren, and Lauter in 2009, when they constructed the RM-CGL hash function on these graphs and proved that they are Ramanujan. As a consequence, these graphs enjoy optimal expansion properties, which are either absent or difficult to establish in other higher-dimensional isogeny graphs. In this paper, we take a closer look at these graphs from a cryptographic perspective, and attempt to demonstrate that they are the natural generalization of the supersingular $\ell$-isogeny graph to dimension two. To this end, we tackle two algorithmic problems: We design and implement the RM-KLPT algorithm to solve the algebraic pathfinding problem in these isogeny graphs by solving a norm equation in ideals of a quaternion algebra over a real quadratic field. Further, we revisit the RM-CGL hash function, provide a proof-of-concept implementation, and showcase that knowledge of the initial surface's algebraic description leads to a second-preimage attack on the hash function through our RM-KLPT algorithm. RM-KLPT resembles the one-dimensional KLPT algorithm much more closely than KLPT$^2$ does. This is due to the existence of a higher-dimensional analogue of the Deuring correspondence in the RM setting, which yields significantly shorter paths ($\sim p^{3}$) compared to KLPT$^2$. Finally, we conclude by discussing potential cryptographic constructions that may be built from RM-KLPT.

item.title: Provably Subexponential Algorithms for Bounded-Error LWE with Few Samples
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2426
Authors: Haoxing Lin, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan
Summary: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size $n$ over prime moduli $q=n^{\kappa+o(1)}$, for any fixed $\kappa>0$, with errors bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, in time $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$ given $n+O(n/\ln\ln n)$ original samples. Further, if each coordinate of the secret is also bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, the same time bound holds with errors bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ and only $O(n/\ln\ln q)$ samples.
Earlier, it was known that Kirchner and Fouque's algorithm could solve LWE with these parameters in subexponential time with a much larger number of samples $m = \Omega(n\log{n})$ [HKM18]. Ducas et al. [DEL25] showed that an adaptation of this algorithm could solve the corresponding dual, the $\mathrm{SIS}^{\infty}$ problem, with a suitable norm bound $q/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ and $m=n+\omega(n/\ln\ln n)$ variables in subexponential time. Whereas their analysis involves interpreting the algorithm in terms of chains of lattices, our approach is quite elementary and is based on bounding the lower moments of a Fourier statistic.

item.title: Sample-Preserving Search-to-Decision Reduction for Noisy Linear Equations over Large Moduli
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2425
Authors: Andrej Bogdanov, Kel Zin Tan, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan
Summary: The Noisy Linear Equations problem involves finding the solution to a random linear system over a finite field given noisy evaluations. This is a generalisation of various learning problems widely used in cryptography, including Learning with Errors (LWE), Learning with Rounding (LWR), and Learning Parity with Noise (LPN).
We present a new sample-preserving search-to-decision reduction for Noisy Linear Equations that has complexity $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log q, q/\sigma)$, where $n$ is the dimension of the secret, $m$ is the number of samples, $q$ is the modulus, and $\sigma$ is the magnitude of the noise (defined suitably for the kind of noise involved). In particular, this implies search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR that run in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ even if the modulus $q$ is exponentially large, as long as the noise-to-modulus ratio $\sigma/q$ is non-negligible. Our reduction works for prime moduli $q$. If $q$ is composite, it instead produces a list that contains a small multiple of the solution.
Prior to this work, known search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR either did not preserve the parameters of the problem (i.e., $m$, $n$, $\sigma$, and $q$), or had complexity that scaled polynomially with either $\sigma$ or the largest prime factor of $q$.

item.title: Counterexamples to Beyond-Johnson Proximity Gaps over Binary Fields
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2424
Authors: Quang Dao, Scott Duke Kominers, Justin Thaler, Kai Zhe ZHeng
Summary: Many hash-based proof systems check that committed words are close to Reed–Solomon codewords by testing one random combination of them. Their soundness analysis uses a proximity gap: if the combination agrees with a codeword on many positions, so do the original words, on the same positions, except for a few exceptional challenges. Such gaps are known above the Johnson threshold, about $\sqrt\rho$ for rate $\rho$, and extending them below it would shrink proofs. Recent work does so in large characteristic, but not over binary fields, where some of the fastest proof systems run. We show that beyond-Johnson proximity gaps fail over binary fields.
Our first construction applies to any additive domain (a binary linear subspace) filling a constant fraction of a containing binary field. Over a suitable extension challenge field and at rate $1/4$, it gives two words that can simultaneously match codewords on at most $25\%$ of the positions, while their combinations approach the $50\%$ Johnson threshold for superpolynomially many challenges. This rules out any $\mathrm{poly}(N)/|\mathbb F|$ bound on the exceptional probability below Johnson. On Binius64's domain (length $2^{27}$, $128$-bit challenges), the combination reaches $49.4\%$ agreement with probability above $2^{-30}$.
The construction also rules out polynomial-size decoding lists below Johnson: one word agrees with superpolynomially many codewords at agreement approaching $50\%$, whereas earlier superpolynomial lists needed the rate, or the agreement–rate gap, to vanish.
Our second and third constructions cover every additive domain, including the sparse domains used by LeanVM and Flock. At rate $1/16$, the second gives $(N-1)(N-2)/6$ exceptional challenges at the Johnson threshold itself, when the domain lies in a proper subfield of the challenge field. For domains larger than $2^{20}$, this rules out even $90$ bits of soundness from a single beyond-Johnson proximity-gap check over a $128$-bit challenge field.
The third construction trades agreement for larger exception counts: at rate $1/2$ and length $2^{22}$, its combinations reach $53.125\%$ agreement from common agreement $50\%$, with probability at least $2^{-20}$ over a $192$-bit challenge field. Finally, at every fixed rate, some constant agreement above the rate makes every challenge exceptional, over $\mathrm{poly}(N)$-size challenge fields. All of our results are formally verified in Lean.

item.title: Magnetar: High-speed post-quantum RV64 zkVM from standard hashes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2423
Authors: Srinath Setty
Summary: We describe the design, implementation, and experimental evaluation of Magnetar, a transparent proof system for RV64I program executions (i.e., a zkVM). Magnetar is the first zkVM to simultaneously satisfy the following three properties:
1. General-purpose proving. Magnetar proves programs compiled to the general-purpose RV64I ISA. An implementation of the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) written in Rust or Go can therefore run inside Magnetar, yielding a zkEVM for proving executions of existing EVM smart contracts.
2. Hash-based, post-quantum security. Magnetar’s cryptographic security is rooted in standard hash functions (e.g., SHA-256 or SHA-3).
3. Efficient recursion. Magnetar’s verification work is dominated by evaluating standard hash functions. Magnetar’s proof engine, BinarySpartan, is well-suited for such bit-oriented computations, so verifying a proof is itself an efficient proving workload.
Unlike prior general-purpose zkVMs, Magnetar does not rely on circuit-friendly algebraic hash functions such as Poseidon or Poseidon2, elliptic-curve or lattice assumptions, or a conjectured Reed–Solomon proximity gap. Even prior zkVMs commonly described as hash-based rely on elliptic-curve or lattice assumptions in their core proving machinery, provide only about 100 bits of security, or rest on conjectured soundness; some do more than one of these.
Finally, we implement Magnetar in Rust and experimentally evaluate it. We find that, at 120 bits of provable security and with 12 performance cores on an M4 Max MacBook Pro, Magnetar proves 2^{22}-cycle executions at 7.2–8.7 million cycles per second, with proofs of about 600 KiB that verify in 11–13 ms. Across 15 application workloads, Magnetar’s proving throughput is 24–66× that of SP1 Hypercube, a hash-and-more-based zkVM; 12–37× that of Jolt-Dory, a curve-based zkVM; and 6–20× that of Jolt-Akita, a lattice-based zkVM, with geometric-mean speedups of about 39×, 18×, and 9.6×, respectively. An optimized Magnetar proves 222-cycle executions at 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each geometric-mean speedup by about 1.3×. Magnetar’s proofs are about 4.6× smaller than SP1 Hypercube’s; Jolt’s proofs are under 100 KiB, but they rely on elliptic-curve or lattice assumptions.
